claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 can be produced with a well-characterized hierarchical heterostructure containing nanoscale precipitates and microscale grain-boundary features.
The specified HfNbTiVAl10 hierarchical heterostructure is in an equilibrium state.

Integrating in situ high-resolution microstructural imaging with supervised machine learning will predict Young’s modulus in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately and rapidly than established continuum simulations.
The imaging-and-ML framework will predict yield strength in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately and rapidly than established continuum simulations.
The imaging-and-ML framework will predict fracture behavior in hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 more accurately and rapidly than established continuum simulations.
The spatial distribution of grain boundaries, phase interfaces, and nanoscale precipitates governs local stiffness variations.
The spatial distribution of grain boundaries, phase interfaces, and nanoscale precipitates governs stress concentrations.
The spatial distribution of grain boundaries, phase interfaces, and nanoscale precipitates governs crack initiation.
A supervised machine-learning model can use captured microstructural features to statistically relate local heterogeneities to macroscopic mechanical responses.
Using microstructural features in the machine-learning model will reduce computational complexity and bypass extensive traditional simulation pathways.
The ML framework will reduce mechanical-property prediction error by approximately 10–20% relative to conventional simulations.
The ML framework will reduce computation time by at least 30% relative to conventional simulations.
Significant microstructural evolution during testing may cause the predictive approach to fail.
Substantial deviation of test-set heterostructures from those represented in the training data may cause the predictive approach to fail.
High strain rates or elevated temperatures may produce significant microstructural evolution in this material during testing.
The relevant established baselines include finite-element models using homogenized material properties and classical fracture models.
